extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of 19th-century American correspondence; historians researching Mary Lincoln, Elizabeth Keckley, Frederick Douglass, and period fundraising/press practices
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards embedded in 19th‑century correspondence about organizing a public subscription/fundraising campaign and handling the sale/exhibition of a widow's personal effects, including publicity management and financial settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundraising lectures should be on a grand scale
rubrics_metrics.description: If lectures are used to raise funds, they should not be a small ad hoc series; the enterprise 'should be done on a grand scale' and should secure the best speakers in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'I doubt the wisdom of getting up a series of lectures for that purpose; that is just the last thing that should be done. Still, if the thing is done, it should be done on a grand scale. The best speakers in the country should be secured for the purpose.' Also: avoid assigning supposedly token positions that 'give color' to the idea (e.g., don't place a Black speaker conspicuously at head/foot—'sandwich me between').

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate meetings and simultaneous movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put only a fraction of your force into the field; meetings (e.g., Cooper Institute) should be held in concert with other movements so the effort is not isolated and vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'that meeting should only be held in concert with other movements. It is bad generalship to put into the field only a fraction of your army when you have no means to prevent their being cut to pieces.' Ensure simultaneous/related actions to maximize impact and protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue circulars and secure wide publicity before key dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely wide circulation (circulars, newspaper blasts, placarding) is essential—circulars should go out early (e.g., before an election) to build momentum and avoid giving opponents time to gather strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'Let Mr. Brady out with his circulars, with his list of commanding names, let the Herald and Tribune give a united blast upon their bugles, let the city be placarded...' Mrs. Lincoln: circulars 'must be sent out before the election'—delay can ruin prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include prominent, trusted names on circulars to give character
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulars and publicity must carry the names of prominent, trusted individuals to lend responsibility and credibility to the movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: Brady & Keyes were 'unable to obtain the names of prominent men, whom the people had confidence in, for the circular, to give character and responsibility to the movement'—their failure to do so undermined the campaign. Douglass and Greeley commentary emphasize the same point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place management in hands of a recognized, responsible leader
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns and collections should be managed by a known, solid, and trusted person whose reputation assures contributors their money is safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass/Greeley: 'The whole thing should be in the hands of some recognized solid man in New York. No man would be better than Mr. Greeley... a dollar placed in his hands would be as safe... everybody believes this.' Choosing the right manager increases public confidence and chances of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reporter publicity for sensitive personal meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Private interviews or meetings (e.g., with the widow) should be conducted quietly to prevent reporters from turning them to the subject's prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'I would gladly see Mrs. Lincoln, if this could be done in a quiet way without the reporters getting hold of it, and using it in some way to the prejudice of that already much abused lady.' Control media exposure for delicate interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not launch inadequate or poorly organized efforts that risk ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: A failed or halfhearted initial public effort will make the cause ridiculous and irreparably damage its prospects; ensure adequate preparation and support before public launch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'Don't let the cause be made ridiculous by failure at the outset... the cause could not be damaged by any such generalship, which would place us in the van unsupported.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace ineffective agents and ensure energetic management
rubrics_metrics.description: If appointed agents (e.g., Brady & Keyes) are slow, ineffective, or fail to act, find someone else to run the machinery—delay and slowness harm the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Douglass: 'If Mr. Brady does not for any reason find himself able to move the machinery, somebody else should be found to take his place; he made a good impression on me when I saw him, but I have not seen the promised simultaneous movement...' Mrs. Lincoln likewise criticizes 'slow, bad management.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the subject's reputation by restricting printed statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow publication of the subject's letters or statements without consent; manage authorship and attribution of public statements carefully to avoid misuse and abuse by opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Lincoln: 'Tell Mr. Brady and Keyes not to have a line of mine once more in print.' Later: 'My authority must not be given... It must be managed very judiciously, and without a day's delay.' Also instructions to show sensitive notes only to specific people and then destroy them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sensitive documents and counter falsehoods promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit circulation of potentially damaging printed items, share them only with trusted agents, and destroy copies after use; actively counter false rumors and press attacks to protect the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Lincoln: 'Show the note enclosed with this to B. & K.; do not let them retain it an instant after reading, nor the printed articles. Let no one see them but themselves, and then burn them.' She also urges timely replies and management of press scraps to prevent harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect goods from unauthorized exhibition and ensure consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow exhibition of a widow's wardrobe or personal goods in other cities without her consent; unauthorized exhibitions risk humiliation and damage to the subject's dignity and to the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: 'A portion of the wardrobe was then taken to Providence, to be exhibited, but without her consent.' City authorities prevented it; the narrator judged that had it succeeded it would have led to a travelling show exposing the wardrobe for admission—an outcome to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and return fine unsold items; avoid soiling or damage
rubrics_metrics.description: When selling or exhibiting personal garments, protect the finest items from being sold or soiled; arrange packing and return of specified valuable items if they cannot be sold acceptably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Lincoln provides a detailed list of items she wishes returned if not sold (e.g., camel's hair shawls, bracelets, sable cape). She instructs 'The lace dress, flounce, and shawl, if there is no possibility of their being sold... return me... all other fine articles.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain detailed invoices and formal full-settlement receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep careful accounts of items invoiced and sold and demand a written, dated receipt stating full payment 'in full of all demands of every kind up to date' to close the business properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: The firm sent an invoice listing items and charges 'amounted to eight hundred dollars.' Mrs. Lincoln sent a check; the narrator 'demanded and received a receipt worded as follows: "Received... eight hundred and twenty dollars in full of all demands of every kind up to date."' This closed the business.
